extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements supply an 'inventive concept' (i.e., amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception) under Alice/Mayo Step 2B, with a focus on MPEP §2106.05(a) (improvements to computer/technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Do additional elements amount to an inventive concept (significantly more)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)? Examiners should answer this by first identifying additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is made with respect to considerations the Supreme Court identified and discussed in the MPEP (§2106.05(a)-(h)). This is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and determine whether they encompass an inventive concept. If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Pathway C). If not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should identify any additional element(s) beyond the judicial exception(s) (carried over from Step 2A Prong Two) and evaluate those elements both individually and in combination to determine contribution to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry over identification of additional elements and conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two (including considerations discussed in MPEP §§2106.05(a)-(c),(e),(f),(h)). Re-evaluate any element or combination previously considered 'insignificant extra-solution activity' (per §2106.05(g)), because re-evaluation may find the element unconventional or more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Also evaluate whether elements merely append well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level per §2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each claim separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application; a dependent claim may recite additional elements that amount to significantly more even if an independent claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome rule: Pathway C eligibility vs 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole recites significantly more than the exception, the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception, the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concluding there is no inventive concept, formulate an ineligibility rejection per MPEP §2106.07. If there is an inventive concept, the eligibility analysis is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2106.05(a): Improvements to functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patent eligibility, examiners should consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.' This consideration is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem and may be evaluated at Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration has support in case law (e.g., Enfish, McRO, DDR Holdings, Amdocs). If an asserted improvement is to conventional computer functioning or technology, the specification must provide technical explanation of how to implement the invention so that a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. Improvements that are merely assertions without technical detail are insufficient. The examiner should analyze both the specification and the claim to ensure the claim reflects the disclosed improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must provide technical explanation showing asserted improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is asserted the invention improves conventional functioning of a computer or technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not explicitly use the word 'improvement,' but must describe the invention such that the improvement is apparent to one of ordinary skill. Conclusory statements asserting an improvement without necessary detail are insufficient (e.g., contrast McRO (sufficient explanation) with Affinity Labs (insufficient details)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement; evaluate the claim 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding the specification discloses an improvement, ensure the claim itself reflects that improvement: the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement (though it need not literally recite the improvement phrase). Evaluate the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not oversimplify claims or ignore specific claim requirements. A claimed improvement must be present in the claim scope; mere recitation of generic computer components may be insufficient even if the specification describes improvements (see Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement may arise from one or more additional elements or their combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement can be provided by one or more additional elements, or by additional element(s) in combination with the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claims as a whole for unconventional, non-generic arrangements of elements (e.g., BASCOM installation/location/combination example). See Diamond v. Diehr and Finjan/Finjan-related discussion in MPEP §2106.04(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant evidence and 37 CFR 1.132 practice when examiner finds no improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner concludes the disclosed invention does not improve technology, the burden shifts to the applicant to provide persuasive arguments supported by any necessary evidence (e.g., declarations) to demonstrate that one of ordinary skill would understand the disclosure as improving technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 must establish what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill and cannot be used to supplement the specification. Declarations may testify to how an ordinarily skilled artisan would interpret the disclosure, but cannot add missing technical detail to the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-limited scope requirement and mental-steps/telephone/verbal embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; a claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed process covers embodiments that are performable without a computer (e.g., verbally or by telephone), it cannot improve computer technology (see Synopsys; RecogniCorp). Ensure claim scope excludes purely mental or non-computer implementations when asserting computer-functionality improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples the courts have indicated may show an improvement in computer-functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The guideline lists illustrative examples of improvements courts have found persuasive (e.g., modification of hyperlink protocol for dual-source hybrid webpage; inventive distribution of functionality to filter Internet content; methods of rendering halftone images; distributed network architectures reducing congestion; memory systems configurable by processor type; technical details for transmitting images; particular server structures storing organized images; particular software programming/menus; methods generating security profiles; improved user interfaces; interfaces for navigating 3D spreadsheets; licensed-software operation restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples (enumerated i–xii in the MPEP) are illustrative, not exhaustive, and show the kinds of unconventional technical solutions courts have recognized as improvements. Use these as analogies when assessing whether a claimed element(s) plausibly provides a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples the courts have indicated may NOT be sufficient to show an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The guideline lists illustrative examples courts have found insufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality (e.g., functionally claimed restaurant menus; accelerating analysis solely by general-purpose computer speed; mere automation of manual processes; recording/transmitting/archiving images with conventional tech; affixing barcodes without technical details; instructions to display information without how-to limitations; improving stored information quality rather than database functionality; arranging GUI information to assist users).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples (enumerated i–viii) indicate shades of insufficient technical contribution: merely using generic computer capabilities, asserting speed gains due solely to a general-purpose computer, or claiming results without technical means to achieve them will typically fail to supply an inventive concept. Compare claim specifics to these examples when deciding insufficiency.
